title: Rub it in, not on
text:
The massage matters as much as what is in the jar.

A dab of rub sitting on your skin does very little. Rub it in with slow, firm circles for a good 20 seconds. Massage warms the area, eases the tightness around the sore spot, and helps the herbs absorb.

Try it like this:
A small amount on your fingertips.
Slow circles, firm enough to move the skin.
Work outward from the sore spot.
Wash your hands after, and keep it away from your eyes.

If a pain is sharp, getting worse, or came from a fall or a big knock, see your GP before you start rubbing.

We filmed this with the Sports Rub, and the same goes for every rub in the range. Save this one for later.

title: Stock the summer first-aid kit
text:
A good summer first-aid kit lives where the injuries happen: the bach, the car and the sports bag.

Here is what goes in ours.
For cuts and blisters: plasters, blister pads, strapping tape, antiseptic wipes and tweezers.
For sprains and knocks: a crepe bandage, an instant ice pack, and the number for the nearest medical centre written down. Phone signal at the bach is not a given.
For the days after: a rub for tired muscles, bumps and bruises. Relief for the family, Sports for the ones who overdo it. Roll-ons fit a glovebox.

If a knock is serious, the kit is not the answer. See your GP or call 111.

title: Herb two: Horopito, the pepper tree
text:
Horopito is the native pepper tree, and the name tells you why: bite a leaf and it bites back.

It is a small shrub with red-blotched leaves that grows in our forests from the North Island hills down to Stewart Island. In rongoā rākau, Māori plant medicine, horopito was traditionally used for the skin and for circulation. That warming quality is what drew us to it.

Today it sits in our {RANGE} range, working alongside other native herbs. No single herb does the job on its own, which is why each of our jars holds 11 to 14 active ingredients, where most rubs use 5 or 6.

title: Jess: why we started X-ZONE
text:
We get asked this a lot, so Jess answers it herself.

We have been friends since we met at primary school in West Auckland, aged six, with the Waitākere Ranges on our doorstep. After years in corporate jobs, Jess in commercial real estate and Dan in advertising, we wanted to do something more meaningful.

So we bought a small business from a horse trainer. She had made a rub for her race horses' tight, sore muscles, and when friends and family kept asking for "that horse stuff", she made one for people. We did a rongoā course, did our research, and reformulated it. The original had two native herbs, harakeke and kūmarahou. Today there are eleven, across three ranges.

That is still the whole idea. Move freely, live naturally.

Got a question for Jess or Dan? Ask it in the comments and we may answer it on camera.

title: Five things for a tramper's kit
text:
Five things in a tramper's first-aid kit, and number four is a roll-on.

1. Blister care: plasters, strapping tape and small scissors. Treat hot spots early.
2. A crepe bandage for a rolled ankle or a sore knee on the way down.
3. A survival blanket. December weather in the hills still turns.
4. A roll-on for tight calves and sore feet at the end of the day. Our Sports roll-on fits the lid pocket.
5. A plan someone else knows. Leave your intentions at home and carry a locator beacon on remote tracks.

And know when to turn back. If someone can't bear weight, has knocked their head, or is cold and confused, stop and get help.

title: Herb three: Kūmarahou, gumdiggers' soap
text:
Kūmarahou is known as gumdiggers' soap. Crush the flowers with a little water and they lather in your hands, which is how the old gumdiggers washed up in the north.

It is a native shrub that grows on poor clay soils, mostly in the upper North Island, and it flowers pale yellow in spring. In rongoā rākau, Māori plant medicine, kūmarahou has a long history of traditional use.

It is herb three in our series, and you will find it in our Joints and Sports ranges.

title: Mavis and Pam on the Joints Rub
text:
Stiff joints are often worst first thing in the morning and after sitting still, and they can make summer feel smaller: shorter walks, less time in the garden.

What helps alongside a rub:
Move little and often. Short walks beat one long one.
Warmth for morning stiffness: a warm shower before you get going.
Keep the muscles around the joint strong with gentle exercise.

If a joint is suddenly hot, red and swollen, or the pain keeps you up at night, see your GP.

Two of our customers put it in their own words. Mavis from Huntly: "Excellent for my arthritis." Pam from Balclutha: "Excellent for my rheumatics."

Their words, not a promise: every body is different. Our Joints Rub is our higher-strength rub for stiffness and mobility, made with native herbs traditionally used for pain. Link in bio.

title: Bumps, bruises and grazes
text:
Summer holidays bring scraped knees and the odd bump on the head. Most are normal. A few need a doctor.

Normal: a bump or bruise with some swelling that changes colour over a week or two, and a graze that looks a little better each day. Cold pack in the first 48 hours. Clean grazes with water and cover them.

See your GP if they can't bear weight, a limb looks misshapen, pain gets worse after 48 hours, or a graze shows spreading redness, heat or pus.

After a head knock, watch for vomiting, drowsiness, confusion or a worsening headache. That is a 111 call or a trip to A and E.

For everyday bumps and bruises on unbroken skin, our Relief Rub is suitable from age five.

title: Herb five: Koromiko
text:
Koromiko grows almost everywhere in Aotearoa, from roadside banks to the edge of the bush. Ask an older Kiwi and there is a good chance they remember it.

It is a native hebe, with long narrow leaves and white to lilac flower spikes in summer. In rongoā Māori the leaves were traditionally used for upset stomachs, and on the skin for cuts and sores. During the Second World War, families even sent dried koromiko to soldiers overseas.

title: Backyard cricket warm-up
text:
Most backyard cricket injuries happen in the first over. Cold muscles, a big lunch and one heroic dive.

Twenty seconds is all it takes:
1. Ten arm circles each way, small to big.
2. Six walking lunges each side, with a twist.
3. Side shuffles across the lawn, then three easy run-ups before you bowl flat out.

It matters most for anyone who has not played since last summer, or who has an old shoulder or knee that likes to complain. Start slow, then build up.

If you go down hard and something swells fast, or you cannot put weight on it, get it checked by your GP or an after-hours clinic.

title: Boxing Day recovery guide
text:
Muscle aches the day after Christmas are often less about the cricket and more about the heat, the sun and the extra glass of bubbles. Even mild dehydration can leave muscles tight, crampy and sore.

title: The 10% rule for January
text:
Most January injuries are not bad luck. They are too much, too soon.

The 10% rule is simple: increase your weekly training by no more than about 10%, whether that is minutes walked, kilometres run or kilos lifted. Muscles adapt quickly. Tendons, ligaments and joints take longer, and that gap is where the trouble starts.

It matters even more if you are coming back after years off, carrying an old injury or living with arthritis. Slow progress is still progress, and it keeps you out on the track.

If pain changes how you move, comes with swelling or lasts more than a week, see your GP or physio.

title: Herb six: Pūriri
text:
Pūriri grows in the forests of the upper North Island, and it flowers almost all year round. If you have seen kererū and tūī busy in one tree in midwinter, there is a good chance it was a pūriri.

title: A weekly recovery routine
text:
Recovery is not what you do once you are hurt. It is what you do every week so you are less likely to get hurt.

3. Massage the sore spots. A few minutes after training or before bed.

If an ache turns into sharp pain or swelling, see your GP or physio before you push on.

title: DOMS explained
text:
The soreness that turns up two days after a big session has a name: DOMS, delayed onset muscle soreness.

When you ask muscles to do something new or harder, tiny strains appear in the fibres. Repairing them, and the inflammation that comes with it, takes time, which is why day two often hurts more than day one. It is not lactic acid. That clears quickly.

What helps: keep moving gently, drink water, eat some protein, sleep well and massage the sore muscles. Massage is where a rub like our Sports Rub fits in.

If you have sharp pain, swelling, soreness that is still getting worse after three days, or dark urine, stop and see your GP.

Save this for your first week back.

title: Heat or ice, answered
text:
Heat or ice? The honest answer is that it depends on how new the pain is.

Ice is for new injuries. A fresh sprain, a knock or anything swelling in the first 48 hours. Wrap it in a cloth and keep it on for 15 to 20 minutes, never straight on the skin.

Heat is for stiffness. A tight lower back, a sore neck, muscles that ache after a long day. Warmth helps them relax.

Joints are where it gets personal. Morning stiffness and arthritis often feel better with warmth. A joint that is hot, red and swollen usually prefers cool, and a sudden hot, swollen joint is worth a GP visit.

Never put heat on fresh swelling, and never fall asleep on a heat pack.

For the everyday aches in between, our rubs are made to be massaged in. Save this.

title: Lower back on site
text:
Most lower back pain on site builds slowly. Small habits stop it building.

Five that cost nothing:
1. Warm up for two minutes before the first lift.
2. Keep the load close and turn with your feet.
3. Change position every 30 minutes.
4. Ask for a hand with the heavy stuff.
5. Look after the drive home and your sleep.

If your back pain comes with numbness, weakness, pain down a leg, or any change to your bladder or bowel, see your GP straight away. That is not one to rub and wait on.

For the everyday ache after a long day, a proper massage with a rub helps you wind down. Our Joints and Sports rubs are made with native NZ herbs, 11 to 14 active ingredients in every jar.

title: Medicines linked to muscle pain
text:
If a new medicine and new muscle aches arrived at the same time, they might be connected.

Some common medicines are linked to muscle pain as a side effect: statins for cholesterol, some antibiotics, longer courses of steroid tablets, and a few others. It doesn't happen to everyone, and it's often easy to sort.

The most important thing: don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Write down when the aches started, then talk to your GP or pharmacist. They can check the dose or suggest another option.

For everyday comfort while you sort it out, a gentle massage with a natural rub can help. Please check with your pharmacist that it suits you alongside your medicines.

The full list of seven is on our blog. Link in bio.

title: Tūpākihi, herb ten
text:
Tūpākihi is the herb most people have never heard of, and the one with some of the most interesting lab results.

It's herb ten of our eleven, and it lives in our Joints Rub. In independent lab tests (Trinity Bioactives), Tūpākihi oil reduced COX-2 activity, a pathway linked to inflammation, by 28.4%. That was a test on cells, not people, so we share it as what it is: an encouraging early result.

One important thing: the wild plant is poisonous. Please never pick it, eat the berries or make anything from it at home.

Tūpākihi is traditionally used in rongoā rākau. Our Joints Rub is made for stiffness and the long-term aches that come with it.

title: Sleep is recovery
text:
Your body does most of its repair while you sleep. No product beats a good night.

Three habits that help most:
1. Same wake time every day, weekends too.
2. A cool, dark, quiet room, with the phone out of reach.
3. Thirty minutes of wind-down before bed, off screens.

Where does a rub fit? As part of that wind-down. A slow massage into whatever aches tells your body the day is over.

"I've never slept like this." Tracey, New Zealand.

If pain wakes you most nights, or you're tired no matter how long you sleep, talk to your GP. It's worth getting checked.

title: Long weekend first aid
text:
Long weekends bring long drives, new tracks and backyard games. Here's what to do in the first 48 hours if something hurts.

Rolled ankle: rest it, ice wrapped in a cloth for 15 to 20 minutes, a firm bandage, and keep it raised.
Bumps and bruises: cold first, then a gentle massage with a rub once the swelling settles.
Stiff after the drive: stop every two hours, walk and stretch.

If you can't put weight on it, the pain is severe, or something looks out of shape, see a doctor or call Healthline on 0800 611 116.

Our Relief range is the one for the bach or the car, for the bumps once the swelling settles.

However you spend the weekend, we hope it is a good one with whānau. Save this for the drive.

title: Trials warm-up for kids
text:
Most trial-day ankle and knee injuries happen in the first ten minutes, before muscles are warm.

A 20-second warm-up kids can do on their own:
High knees.
Side shuffles.
Calf raises.
Small hops, landing soft with knees over toes.

Then a few minutes of easy jogging and passing before the trial starts. Landing soft and keeping the knees in line with the toes is the habit worth teaching early.

If an ankle or knee swells, or your child can't put weight on it, stop and get it checked by a doctor or physio.

Good luck to everyone trialling this week. Save this for the car park.
